method: Each answer key and rationale read against the pinned texts in data/sources/; supporting passages quoted verbatim into the bank. status: ok = key and rationale supported; unsourced = no pinned text decides it (note names the document that would). fixed = rationale or option corrected in this pass.

1001.note: Art 114 TFEU legal basis (Recital 3) and risk-based approach (Recital 26); NLF alignment stated in Recital 9.

1002.note: Recital 12 speaks only of alignment with 'the work of international organisations working on AI'; it never names the OECD. The OECD link is stated in the Commission Guidelines on the definition of an AI system (C(2025) 924, Feb 2025), which we do not hold. Explain text overstates Recital 12; suggest: 'Recital 12 requires close alignment with the work of international organisations; the Commission's February 2025 guidelines identify this as the OECD definition...'. Also the claim that the Council of Europe Convention 'postdates' the Act is shaky (Convention adopted 17 May 2024, AI Act signed 13 June 2024); suggest dropping 'postdates and'.

1004.note: Border control is Annex III point 7; open-source high-risk systems stay in scope under Art 2(12).

1006.note: Key (a) is correct, but the explanation's last sentence 'A completed FRIA is irrelevant to a practice governed by Art 5' is contradicted by Art 5(2), which makes a completed Art 27 FRIA (and EU database registration) a condition for authorising real-time RBI. Proposed replacement: 'A completed FRIA is a precondition under Art 5(2), not a substitute for the exception and prior authorisation, so option C misdescribes the regime.'

1007.note: Remote biometric identification is Annex III point 1(a); Art 5(1)(h) covers only 'real-time' use.

1012.note: Point (bb) covers child sexual abuse material within Directive 2011/93/EU. 27 July 2026 is the Omnibus's entry into force (third day after publication on 24.7.2026; Art 4), cf. Art 1(40)(c) 'Articles 102 to 110 shall apply from 27 July 2026'.

1013.note: Machinery Regulation 2023/1230 moved to Annex I Section B point 21 (Art 1(41)(b)); safety-component test narrowed via Art 3(14) and new Art 6(1a)-(1c). Strictly, the component is high-risk only if it is a safety component of machinery needing third-party assessment; option a remains the only defensible answer.

1014.note: Art 6(3)-(4) and 49(2) not amended by the Omnibus.

1015.note: Option c says 'transport' where Annex III point 2 says 'road traffic'; close enough not to be a correct answer.

1019.note: Key (a) correct. Explanation's claim that NIS2 and the CRA 'can support but not replace the Art 15 assessment' is contradicted for the CRA: CRA Art 12(1) and new AI Act Art 42(3) (Omnibus) deem CRA-compliant high-risk AI products to meet the Art 15 cybersecurity requirements. Proposed replacement for the last sentence: 'Generic network and organisational security belongs to NIS2 and the Cyber Resilience Act; for products in CRA scope, meeting the CRA essential requirements is deemed to satisfy the Art 15 cybersecurity requirement (CRA Art 12, AI Act Art 42(3)), though not accuracy and robustness.'

1020.note: Key (a) correct. Explanation's 'the AI Office never certifies systems' is outdated: new Art 75(1e) makes the AI Office responsible for third-party conformity assessments of high-risk systems within its exclusive competence (GPAI-based systems from the model provider, VLOP/VLOSE systems), entrusted to notified bodies. Proposed replacement: '...; the AI Office does not certify ordinary Annex III systems, its Art 75(1e) role being limited to third-party assessments of systems under its exclusive competence.'

1021.note: CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 reference not in pinned sources (contextual).

1022.note: Art 16(f) conformity assessment, (g) declaration, (h) CE marking, (i) registration.

1026.note: Omnibus amended only Art 27(4)-(5) (DPIA cross-referencing, template).

1027.note: Benefits eligibility is Annex III point 5(a).

1031.note: Art 53(1)(a) technical documentation, (b) downstream information. July 2025 template date not in pinned sources (apply-ai confirms the Commission adopted the template, undated).

Proposed last sentence: 'Where the system is also a product with digital elements meeting the Cyber Resilience Act's essential requirements, it is deemed to comply with the Art 15 cybersecurity requirements (CRA Art 12(1); AI Act Art 42(3)), but accuracy and robustness must still be shown under the AI Act.'

2003.note: Key (b) supported: Art 70(1)/(3) require designation and resourcing; the omnibus recital itself cites delayed establishment of national competent authorities. The explanation's 'only a minority had both in place' is a figure from Commission monitoring we don't hold (not contradicted). Regulation needs no transposition (final clause: binding and directly applicable).

2006.note: Published 24.7.2026 + third day = 27 July 2026, matches stem. Art 113 third para point (b) (Chapter V from 2 Aug 2025) is not replaced. Optional enrichment: the Omnibus did not merely leave Art 5 in place — it added new prohibitions (Art 5(1)(ba)/(bb), non-consensual intimate material and CSAM) applying from 2 December 2026.

2007.note: Key (b) correct. Explanation's rationale is not what the sources say: the aviation changes are a 'technical correction' so implementing/delegated acts under 2018/1139 take the AI Act's Chapter III Section 2 requirements into account (Recital 44, Art 2), and machinery moved from Annex I Section A to Section B with AI requirements to be built into the Machinery Regulation's Annex III (Recital 42, Art 3) — neither is about 'referencing the original high-risk dates'. Proposed explain: 'Articles 2 and 3 of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amend the EASA Basic Regulation (so that acts on AI safety components take the AI Act's high-risk requirements into account) and the Machinery Regulation (which moves to Section B of AI Act Annex I and must absorb AI health-and-safety requirements by delegated acts applying by 2 August 2028). The data and platform acquis was not touched by this instrument.'

2008.note: Key (a) supported. The SMC thresholds in the explanation (<750 staff, €150m turnover / €129m balance sheet) come from Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099, which we don't hold — not verified here.

2011.note: Key (a) is the best answer, but its wording is inaccurate: the DGA has a notification regime for data intermediation services (Art 11) but a voluntary REGISTRATION regime for recognised data altruism organisations (Arts 17-19), not a notification regime. Proposed option (a): 'a notification regime for data intermediation services and a voluntary registration regime for recognised data altruism organisations'. Art 1(2) ('does not create any obligation on public sector bodies to allow the re-use of data') also rules out (d).

2012.note: Key (c) supported by the legislative definition (also Data Act Recital 103). 'Federated' is not the legislative wording, and the explanation's claims that the EHDS is the first data space in legislation and that a central pool 'was rejected as unworkable' are not in any pinned source (EHDS Regulation (EU) 2025/327 not held); suggest dropping the 'rejected as unworkable' clause.

Nuance: Recital 118 adds that where models are embedded in VLOPs/VLOSEs the corresponding AI Act obligations 'should be presumed to be fulfilled, unless significant systemic risks not covered by Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 emerge'; and the omnibus (Art 75(1)(b)) gives the AI Office exclusive competence over AI systems integrated into VLOPs/VLOSEs. Neither affects the key.

2032.note: Key (d) remains the best answer. But the explanation's 'leaves Union data-protection law untouched' overstates: amended Art 2(7) carves out Art 4a (special-category processing for bias detection, which replaced Art 10(5)) and Art 59 (further processing in sandboxes). Proposed explain: 'Both apply cumulatively: Article 2(7) keeps the GDPR unaffected save for narrow carve-outs in Article 4a (special-category data for bias detection) and Article 59 (sandboxes), and Recital 63 says the Act is not a legal ground for processing unless it specifically provides otherwise. A controller still needs a lawful basis, purpose limitation and, where required, a DPIA. The lex specialis reading is the commonest error: Article 10's data-governance duties are additional to the GDPR, not a substitute for it.'
